title: SEPA: Europe’s unsung hero
gist: OeNB survey data for six SE European countries show remittance recipients still lean on cash and money transfer operators (6-12% cash-to-cash fees vs 1.5-4.5% digital) while SEPA, now 41 countries, is almost free; fewer than 40% have even heard of SEPA, below crypto awareness despite crypto ownership of at most 6%. A 5% fee equals about €140m a year on Bulgaria and €130m on Albania, but account access and weak awareness-to-behavior links limit near-term gains.

insights.claim: Albania's remittance inflows exceed €2.5 billion, about 8.4% of GDP, versus almost €3 billion but only 2.1% of GDP for Bulgaria, so Albania's economy is far more exposed to the cost and reliability of cross-border payment rails.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Remittance-fee and channel shifts are a macro variable for the Western Balkans, not just a consumer issue.

insights.claim: Share of consumers receiving remittances: Albania 21%, Bosnia and Herzegovina 17%, North Macedonia 10%, Serbia 9%, Bulgaria 8%, Romania 4%.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Shows where payment-integration gains would reach the most households.

insights.claim: Across six south-eastern European countries about one-third of remittance recipients get cash via relatives or friends and another third use physical money transfer operators, so the formal bank channel is a minority route.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Large addressable base for bank and fintech rails that can displace cash and MTO flows.
insights.quote: around one-third of recipients receive money in cash via relatives or friends and another third through physical money transfer operators

insights.claim: Only 10-20% of remittance transfers in Bulgaria and Romania are reported as SEPA bank-based transfers, and in the other four countries the majority of transfers are non-SEPA, even though Bulgaria and Romania have been in SEPA scope for over 15 years.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Geographic SEPA membership does not translate quickly into usage.

insights.claim: Cash-to-cash remittances cost roughly 6-12% and digital non-bank transfers 1.5-4.5%, while SEPA transfers are described as almost free, so fees for the same transfer can differ by more than 10 percentage points.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Fee compression is the revenue pool at risk for money transfer operators.

insights.claim: A 5% remittance fee equals roughly €140 million a year on Bulgaria's inflows and €130 million on Albania's, giving an upper-bound sense of household savings from shifting to SEPA.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Savings are an upper bound; real capture depends on behavior change.

insights.claim: SEPA savings are largest when recipients hold euro-denominated accounts, since they avoid currency conversion costs; this links euro adoption (Bulgaria is the newest euro area member) to cheaper remittances.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Euro adoption and euro accounts are an enabler for taking cost out of remittance corridors.

insights.claim: Share of population without a current account or similar product varies widely: Albania about half, Romania 25%, Bosnia and Herzegovina 17%, Bulgaria 10%, Serbia 8%, North Macedonia 2%; SEPA use typically requires a payment account.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Albania's unbanked half caps near-term SEPA benefit; account opening is the gating step.

insights.claim: SEPA now covers 41 countries including all EU members and increasingly EU candidates: Albania and North Macedonia joined in 2024, Serbia in 2025, and Bosnia and Herzegovina applied in August 2026.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: SEPA acts as a payments-level integration path ahead of EU accession.

insights.claim: Joining SEPA's geographic scope does not immediately deliver a fully operational payment system, so consumer benefits lag formal membership.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Expect a delay between accession headlines and actual cost declines.
insights.quote: simply becoming part of SEPA’s geographical scope does not immediately bring with it a fully operational payment system

insights.claim: Fewer than 40% of consumers in surveyed CESEE countries have heard of SEPA, regardless of how long their country has been in scope or recent publicised enlargements.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Infrastructure success is invisible, so public support for integration is hard to build.
insights.quote: fewer than 40% of consumers in the countries surveyed report having heard of it

insights.claim: Awareness of crypto-assets is much higher than awareness of SEPA in the surveyed countries even though no more than 6% of consumers own crypto in any of them.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Mindshare for crypto far exceeds its actual payment or ownership footprint in the region.
insights.quote: awareness of crypto-assets is much higher, although fewer than one in ten consumers own crypto-assets

insights.claim: SEPA awareness rises with income, education and financial literacy; consumers with tertiary education are about 17 percentage points more likely to have heard of it than those with only primary education.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Integration benefits skew toward better-educated households unless outreach is targeted.

insights.claim: The seamlessness of SEPA is what makes it unrecognised: the better cross-border euro payments work, the less consumers think about the infrastructure behind them.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Good payment plumbing builds little political or brand capital.

insights.claim: An information experiment on deposit insurance showed that informing households raised awareness but had little effect on financial choices, implying greater SEPA awareness alone may not shift payment behaviour.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Information campaigns may disappoint; price, access and convenience likely matter more.

insights.claim: Even small shifts in payment channel choice could have tangible household consequences because channel costs differ so much; migrant workers sending money home gain most from switching from cash-to-cash services to SEPA.
insights.speaker: European Central Bank
insights.so_what: Remittance corridors are the highest-yield use case for SEPA outreach and product design.
